title: Teach Your Children How to Cook
author: Jenna A. Robinson
source: Restoring the West by Ayaan Hirsi Ali (www.restoringthewest.com), September 22, 2026
summary: Jenna A. Robinson argues that teaching children to cook prepares them for adulthood, draws families together, and strengthens society. She begins with the family dinner as an anchor of a healthy home and an occasion to unplug, and notes survey evidence that most Americans lack basic kitchen proficiency now that home economics has largely disappeared from schools. Cooking, she contends, is both an economic necessity, as endless takeout is unsustainable, and an act of care and service. She adds that the kitchen is a natural classroom for fractions, proportions, and the physics and chemistry of browning, fermentation, and boiling. The piece closes by linking well-ordered homes to a well-ordered society and urging parents to pass on basic skills and family recipes.
points: Robinson cites a 2024 survey in which 54% of Americans admit they are not proficient in the kitchen, as home economics courses have been cut or made elective.
She frames preparing food as an expression of care and solidarity rather than a mere budget or nutrition question.
Cooking offers built-in lessons in fractions, proportions, weight versus volume, and kitchen physics and chemistry.
The argument ties family dinner and the skills behind it to the sustaining of a well-ordered home and society.
quotes: Regular dinners around the kitchen table bring families together—from young children to teens and parents. They anchor a healthy, happy home.
Home ec courses once gave generations at least some cooking experience. Today, changing school priorities have pushed such courses into electives or eliminated them entirely.
But food is more than just a budget line or a tally of calories and macros. Preparing it expresses care—an act of service and solidarity.
Teaching our children to cook so they can provide for and nourish their own families is one of the most loving things parents can do.
Learning to cook also creates opportunities to teach academic concepts. Measuring ingredients requires an understanding of fractions. Changing the size of a recipe teaches proportions.
Parents who cook and eat with their children pass down family traditions, prepare them for adulthood, and build bonds and memories across generations.
Although learning to cook may never enhance a resume or win a scholarship, it is a fundamental skill every child should learn.
